title: Stoic in grief
hookLine: honest grief, the seasons, sweet memory

cards: Someone at the funeral says it to the dead man's daughter, meaning well: you're being so strong. She hasn't cried in front of anyone. She went back to work on Monday.
People admire it. And at two in the morning, alone in her kitchen, it isn't strength at all. It's a held breath.
That's the common picture of Stoic grief: a stiff upper lip, nothing shown. Seneca's letters paint a different one.

teach.b: Three threads, held together. First, honest grief. Seneca, writing to Lucilius after a friend's death, doesn't tell him not to cry.
The eyes shouldn't be dry when a friend is lost, he says, nor should they overflow: tears are allowed, wailing isn't required.

Then he confesses that when his own friend Annaeus Serenus died, he wept beyond all measure, and counts himself among those whom grief defeated. A teacher who admits that is not asking for stone. Second, the seasons.
The Stoics placed death inside nature's turning, like the ripe olive. That doesn't cancel sorrow.

teach.h: A FRAME BIG ENOUGH FOR SORROW.
teach.b: It's a frame big enough to hold it: leaves fall, and you still miss the green. Seneca, writing to a mother three years into mourning her son, is gentle and patient, and also asks her, slowly, to let her life go on.

Seneca passes on a saying from his teacher Attalus: remembering lost friends can be pleasant, the way some fruits are good because they're a little sharp, or a very old wine has a bitterness that pleases.
Seneca's hope is that the memory of those we've lost becomes a joy, not only a wound.

Put together: tears when they come, a loss held inside the turning year, and, over time, the person coming back as a memory you can visit with something like gladness. Not instead of sorrow. Alongside it.
And today closes a week of carrying the porch into ordinary days.

how: Some readers of Seneca treat grief as something to feel honestly rather than suppress, and over time to turn into grateful memory of the person lost.

o: a Stoic emperor who wrote about grief on campaign
the friend whose death made Seneca weep too much
Seneca's teacher: memories of the lost can turn sweet

s: Seneca told Lucilius never to cry for a lost friend
he said the eyes shouldn't be dry, nor overflowing.
Seneca admitted that grief once defeated him
he wept beyond measure for Annaeus Serenus.
Stoic grief means hiding all feeling
Seneca allowed honest tears and hoped memory would become sweet.

games.q: a close friend has died. you're Seneca, writing to Lucilius about grief. what do you say?
o: weep, but not without end; and I confess I wept too much
forget the friend as fast as you can
games.why: Letter 63: tears are allowed, and Seneca admits he himself was overcome when Serenus died.

practice: Bring to mind one loss, a person, an animal, a place, a time of life, choosing one that feels bearable today; you don't have to open the hardest door.

Let yourself feel what's there, honestly, then let one specific memory come, a voice, a joke, a meal, and hold it like a sharp, sweet fruit. If tears come, they're welcome here; if they don't, that's fine too.

wordCard.voice: Attalus, the teacher whose saying Seneca passed on: that remembering lost friends can turn sweet, like a good bitterness, over time. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: grief, honestly. Tears and gladness can share the same memory. See you tomorrow.
